CausalChain: High inflammatory cytokine levels in the tumor microenvironment -> Activation of PTM-specific enzymes (glycosyltransferases/kinases) -> Induction of distinct glycosylation and phosphorylation modifications on CLDN18.2 -> Disruption of tight junction integrity and enhanced epitope exposure -> Altered binding interfaces on CLDN18.2 -> Improved engagement of immune effectors by CLDN18.2-directed therapies
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in the context of solid tumors with an inflammatory microenvironment, elevated cytokine levels drive the activation of specific enzymes responsible for post-translational modifications, particularly glycosylation and phosphorylation, of CLDN18.2. These modifications lead to the disruption of tight junction integrity and an increase in the exposure and alteration of the protein’s surface epitopes, generating novel binding interfaces. Using modern technological platforms such as proteomic profiling, CRISPR-mediated enzyme screening, and advanced imaging, targeted pharmacological intervention can modulate these PTMs to optimize CLDN18.2’s surface presentation. Consequently, this optimized targetability will synergize with existing CLDN18.2-directed immunotherapies, potentially leading to improved anti-tumor efficacy and clinical outcomes in patients with solid tumors.
Abstract: Recent advances in high-resolution proteomics and CRISPR-based functional screening have enabled a deeper understanding of tumor microenvironment influences on protein post-translational modifications (PTMs). Here, we hypothesize that in solid tumors characterized by high inflammatory cytokine levels, cytokine-induced activation of specific enzymes (such as glycosyltransferases and kinases) results in unique glycosylation and phosphorylation patterns of the tight junction protein CLDN18.2. These PTMs disrupt traditional tight junction integrity, leading to increased surface epitope exposure and the creation of modified binding interfaces. By employing contemporary technologies—including quantitative mass spectrometry, high-resolution imaging, and genome editing—we propose that pharmacological modulation of these enzyme activities can recalibrate CLDN18.2 modifications, thereby enhancing its recognition by CLDN18.2-targeted immunotherapies and improving clinical outcomes in solid tumor treatments.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that inflammation-induced post-translational modifications of CLDN18.2 enhance its surface exposure, thereby improving immune engagement. In the revised hypothesis, we have explicitly incorporated modern technological capabilities (proteomics, CRISPR, advanced imaging) to systematically identify and modulate the specific enzymes (glycosyltransferases and kinases) responsible for these modifications. Additionally, each step of the original causal chain is maintained and refined: (1) high inflammatory cytokines trigger enzyme activation; (2) these enzymes induce altered glycosylation and phosphorylation; (3) the resulting PTMs disrupt tight junctions and enhance epitope exposure; (4) this leads to modified binding characteristics; and (5) ultimately, these changes improve immune effector engagement by targeted therapies. The revised hypothesis offers a more actionable framework by detailing the molecular mechanisms, specifying the PTMs involved, and outlining contemporary experimental approaches for validation.
